title: Chapter 49: Lilies, Part 2 of 5: The Hall of Lilies
html:
The footman in white handed her down from the carriage.
He did not look at her face. He looked at the air above her head, the way they are taught, and held out his white-gloved hand, and she put hers in it, Madame Hesper's wedding glove on his, and stepped down onto the white felt. And then he turned to the carriage again, and braced himself, with his feet apart, because the next one out was the Duke.
It took a long time. It took the footman, and Tibbs, who had come down off the box, and a second footman who came running down the steps. The carriage tipped and groaned. And then the Duke of Marrow was standing on the white felt beside her, enormous, soft, in his dark blue velvet and his white lace and his dove-gray waistcoat with the silver leaves, with his ringed hand on a cane of pale wood topped with a gold ball, breathing a little heavily, and smiling his small sleepy smile at the torches.
He held out his arm.
Lyra took it.
And they went up the white steps together, slowly, at the Duke's pace, between the torches, past the footman in white, under the lily knocker, through the open white door, into the light.
It hit her the way it had hit her in the autumn. The light first, then the heat, then the lilies. All together, through the open door, like a wave breaking over a sea wall. For a moment she could not see. She could only stand on the threshold with her eyes stinging and her throat closing and her gloved hand on the Duke's soft velvet arm, and wait for the world to come back.
It came back in pieces.
The hall. The great tall white hall, so tall the ceiling was lost in a haze of gold. The white marble floor, polished like water, with the lamps upside down in it and her own gray hem. The white walls carved with leaves and ribbons, every leaf and every ribbon picked out in thin gold. The staircase at the far end, going up in two white curving arms, wound from bottom to top with long twisted ropes of lilies. Lilies in the great white urns on either side of the door, taller than a man, leaning out like the spray of a fountain. Lilies on every table, in every vase. Lilies hanging from the gold lamp in the middle of the ceiling in a great white ring, their heavy heads turned down, so that their pollen fell, very slowly, in a fine gold dust, onto the people standing underneath.
And the people.
They filled the hall. A hundred of them. More. The Hill. All of it. In silk and velvet and lace, in every color, with jewels at their throats and their wrists and in their hair, standing in groups on the white marble, talking, laughing, holding glasses of something pale that caught the light. The noise of them was like the noise of the sea in a shell. A soft roar, rising and falling, with sharp bright sounds in it. Laughter. A glass touching a glass. Somebody calling a name.
And as she came through the door on the Duke's arm, the noise stopped.
Not all at once. The way it had stopped in the Duke's drawing room on Saturday. From the door inward. The nearest group first, by the urn, three women in blue and green with feathers in their hair, turning their heads. Then the next. And the next. Across the white marble, back and back, to the foot of the stairs, a long ripple of silence, of heads turning, of glasses stopping halfway to mouths.
She knew them.
She knew every one. Lady Harriet Langley, by the urn, in sky blue, with her mouth open. The two Fennimore boys, by a pillar, in identical bottle-green coats, with identical red faces. The Pellow sisters, all three, in a row, like birds on a fence, in pink and pinker and pinkest. Lord and Lady Ost by the stairs, him gray and bent, her small and sharp and hung all over with garnets. Captain Dray, in his red regimental coat, leaning on the banister with a glass, who had danced with her once at a ball at Crown Walk when she was fifteen and trodden on her foot three times. And old Lady Ashcombe, in black, in a chair by the wall, very upright, with her stick across her knees and a little dog in her lap. Who had turned her back on Lyra on Saturday in the Duke's drawing room, slowly, so that everybody saw.
She did not turn her back now. She looked at Lyra across the white hall with her small black eyes, for a long time. And then she looked at the gray gown. And then, very slightly, Lyra saw her mouth go tight.
She knows the gown, Lyra thought. She knew my mother.
The silence went on.
It was a different silence from Saturday's. She could feel that at once, standing on the threshold on the Duke's arm. On Saturday the silence had been surprise. A Thorne. Here. In that gown. After everything. This was something else. This was the silence of a room that has been talking about you for hours, and has just seen you walk in.
Hesper, she thought. They've been talking about Hesper.
She could hear it in the silence. She could hear what they had been saying a moment ago, before she came in, the way you can hear the shape of a tune in the quiet after it stops. The old dressmaker on Velvet Street. Murdered. Robbers, they say. A girl in gray, over the roofs. Gold dust in the window. They say. They say. They say.
And she was standing in the door, in gray.
The Duke of Marrow, beside her, did not seem to notice anything at all. He stood on the threshold with his cane in one hand and her hand on his other arm, breathing a little heavily from the steps, and looked round the silent hall with his sleepy gray-green eyes, slowly, from face to face, the way a cat looks round a room full of birds.
"Good evening," he said.
He did not say it loudly. He did not need to. The hall was so quiet that his soft purring voice went all the way to the foot of the stairs.
"What a crowd," said the Duke. "And what a smell. Cressida has outdone herself." He smiled his small sleepy smile at Lady Harriet Langley, by the urn, whose mouth was still open. "Harriet, my dear. You look like a fish. Do shut it."
Lady Harriet Langley shut it.
Somebody laughed. One of the Fennimore boys. A short sharp bark of a laugh, quickly swallowed.
And the noise came back.
Not all at once. But it came. Like water coming back into a pool when a stone has been thrown in. Somebody said something to somebody. A glass touched a glass. Captain Dray, on the banister, lifted his own glass toward the Duke, and drank. And the soft roar of the sea in the shell rose up again, and filled the hall, and the heads turned away. Not all the way. Not the eyes. But the heads.
The Duke of Marrow walked her across the white hall.
Slowly. At his pace. Through the crowd, which opened in front of them and closed behind them, the way the clerks on the Ministry Steps open in front of an Inquisitor. Past the urns. Past the Pellow sisters. Past Lady Ashcombe in her chair, who did not turn her back, and did not look away, and watched the gray gown go by with her small black eyes.
To the foot of the stairs.
And stopped there, under the white curving arms of the staircase wound with lilies, with the gold pollen falling down on them from the ring of flowers overhead. And waited.
"She'll come down," said the Duke, very low, out of the side of his mouth, not looking at her. "She always waits until the hall is full. And then she comes down." He smiled at nothing. "Chin up, Lady Lyra. Not too far. Just enough to see the top of the stairs."
Lyra put her chin up.
Just enough.
And at the top of the stairs, where the two white arms met under the gold haze of the ceiling, in a gallery hung with lilies, a door opened.
Cressida
She came down the stairs the way water comes down a slope.
Without hurry, and without stopping, and as if there had never been any question of where she was going. One gloved hand on the white banister among the lilies. The other at her side. White silk, the white of fresh snow, cut close from the shoulders to the hips and then falling away in a long soft rush to the floor, pouring over each step behind her like cream. Long white gloves above the elbow, fastened at the wrist with tiny pearl buttons. Pearls at her throat. Three ropes of them, so close together they looked like a collar.
Her hair was the color of old gold. The gold of coins, of honey held up to a window. Piled high on the back of her head in a great soft shining crown. And through it, holding it, catching the light every time she moved her head, pins. Long ones. Five or six. Long thin silver pins, the kind ladies use to hold a hat on in the wind, pushed through the gold crown of her hair at angles, so that their heads stood out of it like the heads of flowers. And on the end of each one, a bead. Small. Round. White glass. Milky, like a pearl, but brighter. Each one catching the light from the lamps as she came down, and flashing, white, and going dark, and flashing again.
Lyra looked at them.
She did not know why. Something in her looked at them and went still, the way a dog goes still at a sound you cannot hear. White glass beads. On the ends of long pins.
She did not know what it was. She put it away. She would think about it later.
Cressida Thorne reached the bottom of the stairs.
The hall had gone quiet again. Not the silence of before. A different one. The silence of a theater when the curtain goes up. A hundred faces turned toward the stairs. And Cressida stood on the last step, above them all, a little, for a moment, with her gloved hand on the banister and the lilies all round her, and let them look.
She had the Thorne eyes.
Lyra had forgotten that. Or remembered it and put it away. Gray eyes. Clear gray, like rain on a window. Long, and a little slanting at the corners. Lyra's own eyes. Rowan's. Their father's. Looking out of a long fine pale face that was beautiful, and had almost no lines in it at all, though she must have been nearly fifty.
And her mouth was red.
Not pink. Red. Dark, like the inside of a rose. The only color on her. In the middle of all that white.
The red mouth smiled.
And Cressida Thorne came down off the last step, and across the white marble, straight to Lyra, holding out both her gloved hands.
"Lyra," she said.
Softly. Warmly. The way you say the name of somebody you have been missing for a very long time. She took both of Lyra's hands in hers. Madame Hesper's old gloves in Cressida's new ones. She held them. And looked down into Lyra's face, close, so close that Lyra could smell the lilies on her, not the lilies in the hall but her own, thicker, sweeter, coming off her skin and her hair and her pearls. And her gray eyes went bright, and wet.
"Oh, darling," she said. "Oh, darling. You came."
The whole hall was watching. Lyra could feel it. A hundred pairs of eyes on the two of them, on the white and the gray, the aunt and the niece, standing together at the foot of the lily stairs.
She will hold your hands and cry a little and call you darling, the Duke had said, and the whole Hill will see her do it, and that is why she will do it.
"Aunt Cressida," said Lyra.
Her own voice. Polite. Quiet. Steady. She did not know where it came from. She thought perhaps it came from the long gallery at Crown Walk, where she had walked up and down at fourteen with a book on her head while the governess counted.
Cressida's eyes went over her. Quickly. Down and up. The gray silk. The long sleeves. The tiny buttons. Madame Hesper's gloves. The cropped hair, combed flat. They went over all of it the way a buyer's eyes go over a horse at a fair.
And came back up to her face.
"Your hair," said Cressida softly.
"I sold it."
Cressida's red mouth made a small round shape of sorrow.
"Oh, my poor darling," she said. "Oh, my poor brave girl." She squeezed Lyra's hands. "And that gown. I know that gown. That was Isolde's." Her eyes went bright again. "She wore it the night of the Ashcombe ball. The year before she went to the coast. I remember it so clearly. She came down the stairs at Crown Walk in it and your father dropped his gloves." She laughed, the small soft shaken laugh Lyra remembered from the autumn. "Agnes Hesper made it. Poor Agnes."
She said it just like that. In the same soft warm voice. Poor Agnes. Without a pause. Without a flicker. Looking into Lyra's face.
And behind her, across the hall, Lyra heard the silence change.
"You've heard, of course," said Cressida. "About Agnes. Such a terrible thing. Robbers, the Watch says. In her own shop." She shook her head. The white glass beads in her hair flashed. "She dressed me for thirty years, you know. And your mother. And your grandmother before that. And now she's gone. And everything she made is all we have left of her." She looked down at the gray silk. "Like this."
She let go of one of Lyra's hands. Just one. And with her gloved fingers, very lightly, she touched the gray silk at Lyra's waist. On the left side. Where the seam was.
Where the pocket was.
Lyra did not move. She did not breathe. She stood with her aunt's gloved fingertips resting on the silk over Madame Hesper's pocket, over the lily paper folded small inside it, and made her face stay where it was.
Cressida's fingers rested there for a moment.
Then they moved on. Up. To the line of tiny gray buttons. To the sleeve. To the wrist.
"So fine," said Cressida. "Her stitches. Nobody sews like that any more." She took her hand away. "I'm so glad you came, darling. I'm so glad Ansel brought you." She smiled past Lyra at the Duke. "Ansel. You're very wicked. You didn't tell me."
"I never tell you anything, Cressida," said the Duke comfortably. "It's the secret of our friendship."
Cressida laughed.
The whole hall laughed with her. The way a room laughs when it has been told it may.
And under the laughter, still holding Lyra's other hand, Cressida Thorne leaned close, so close that her red mouth was nearly at Lyra's ear, and her lily smell was so thick that Lyra could taste it, and said, very low, in the same soft warm voice, so that nobody else in the whole white hall could hear:
"The tenth bell, darling. Upstairs. The white room. Just the two of us. I've had the cups put out."
The Long Room
The long room was through a pair of white doors on the left of the hall, and it was where the music was.
It ran the whole depth of the house, from the street to the garden, with tall windows at the far end looking out onto the white garden behind, where the snow lay smooth on the paths and the bare trees were hung with little glass lamps like frozen fruit. It was white, like the hall. White walls, white silk on the chairs, white marble at the fireplace. And down the middle of the ceiling, three great chandeliers of glass, each one as big as a carriage wheel, blazing with candles, so that the whole long room swam in a soft trembling gold light.
At the far end, by the windows, four musicians in white coats sat on little gold chairs and played. Two violins, a viola, a cello. Something slow and sweet and old, that Lyra knew and could not name. It went up and down under the talk like the river under a bridge.
And there was a fire. At the middle of the long wall, in a fireplace of white marble carved with lilies, a big fire, burning low and red.
She saw him at once.
She had known she would. The Duke had told her. Standing near the fire, eating very little and listening a great deal. But knowing was not the same.
He was standing to one side of the fireplace, a little apart from everybody, with his back to the white wall. Not tall. Not short. Slight. In a coat of plain dark gray, very good, and a white neckcloth, very plain. Thin fair hair, going gray at the sides. A mild, kind, rather tired face, like a schoolmaster's at the end of a long term. He had a glass in his hand, a tall thin glass of something pale. He did not seem to be drinking it.
He was listening to the music.
His head was a little on one side. His eyes were half closed. And the first finger of the hand that held the glass was moving. Very slightly. On the side of the glass. Lifting, and touching. Lifting, and touching.
Lyra did not count. She did not need to. She had held her brother's hand in a cold stone room at the top of a tower, yesterday, and heard him say it.
Four, and two, and nine, and three.
She looked away.
She made herself look away, slowly, the way you look away from a dog in the street that you do not want to notice you. She looked at the musicians. At the windows. At the white garden with its glass lamps. And when she looked back, out of the edge of her eye, the man by the fire had not moved, and his eyes were still half closed, and his finger was still on the glass.
But his face was turned toward her.
Not his eyes. His face. The way a flower turns toward a window.
The Duke of Marrow was talking to Lord Ost. Something about horses. He had brought her into the long room on his arm and stopped by a white silk sofa near the door, and Lord Ost had come up to him at once, gray and bent, to ask about a gray mare, and the Duke was answering in his slow sleepy purr, and had not let go of her hand on his arm.
Around them, the Hill talked.
She heard it. She could not help hearing. It came at her from every side, in pieces, the way the light came through the chandeliers, broken up and scattered. Women's voices, behind fans. Men's voices, low, by the windows. Not talking to her. Talking near her. Talking the way people talk on the Hill when they know you can hear, and want you to, and will never say so.
—in her own shop, they say. With her shears in her hand.
—a girl in gray, over the roofs, the Watch says. Isn't that—
—Monday, of course. The Masquerade. Everybody will be there. Vivienne has the most extraordinary list this year—
—a Lord's Last Evening. Taken whole. Can you imagine? Whose do you suppose—
—oh, my dear. Whose do you think? Look who she's brought.
—sealed bids. At midnight. They say the Bank has put a clause on it. The Fourth Desk. Nobody may open it but in front of the Auditor—
—the one with the gold tooth? Dreadful woman. She looked at my husband's books last year as if they were something the cat brought in—
Lyra stood very still on the Duke's arm and let it go past her.
Elara, she thought. They mean Elara. Corin's sister. She thought of a cab in the snow, and a woman in a dark green coat with one white glove, and a black box weighed by a bare hand. Corin had told her. She's locked it. Against the Lady. Against us. Against everybody. Except herself.
"Lady Lyra."
A voice at her elbow. Not the Duke's. Light, and easy, and pleasant. The voice of a man who has never had to raise it, because people have always come close enough to hear.
She turned her head.
He was standing beside the white silk sofa, a little behind it, where he had not been a moment ago. A tall man. Not young. Not old. Fifty, perhaps. Lean, and very straight, in a coat of dark gray silk with a thread of silver in it, so fine it was almost not there. A waistcoat of the same gray, cut close. And on the left side of the waistcoat, a deep pocket. And from the pocket, a chain. Gold. Heavy. Looped across to a buttonhole on the other side.
His hair was silver. Not gray. Silver. Thick and smooth and swept back from a high brown forehead, so bright under the chandeliers that it seemed to give off its own light. His face was handsome. Lined at the eyes, the way a face is lined that smiles often and means it some of the time. And his eyes were dark. Very dark. Nearly black. Bright and quick and interested, like the eyes of a bird that has just seen something shining in the grass.
They went over her face. Once. Quickly. Her bare face.
No mask.
And something in them, for a moment, was amused.
"Forgive me," said the man with the silver hair. "We haven't been introduced. And we won't be, I think, not tonight. Cressida would never forgive me." He smiled. A real smile, warm, all the way up to the dark eyes. "I only wanted to say that your mother wore that gown to the Ashcombe ball, the year before she went away. And that I was there. And that nobody in the room looked at anything else all night." He inclined his head. "You'll forgive an old man for saying so."
He did not wait for her to answer.
He turned, and went away down the long room, through the crowd, easily, nodding to people as he went, touching an arm here, a shoulder there, saying a word. And as he went, Lyra saw his hand go to the pocket of his gray waistcoat. To the chain. And rest there, on the gold. On the round shape of the watch inside the pocket.
He did not take it out.
He did not look at it.
He walked away down the long room toward the windows and the music with his hand resting on his watch, and did not look at it once.
Lyra stood on the Duke's arm and watched him go.
Beside her, the Duke of Marrow had stopped talking to Lord Ost about horses. Lord Ost had gone. The Duke was looking down the long room too, after the silver hair, with his sleepy gray-green eyes.
"Dorian," he said softly. "I wondered when he'd find you."
Lyra did not say anything.
"He likes to look at a thing," said the Duke, "before he decides whether to buy it." He patted her hand on his arm. "And he's just seen that you didn't wear his present."
Lyra looked up at him.
The Duke did not look down at her. He was watching the far end of the room, where the silver head had stopped beside the musicians and bent toward the cellist, to say something that made the cellist laugh.
"Oh, yes," said the Duke. "I know about the mask. Everybody who matters on the Hill knows about the mask. Dorian Sterling's footman went to a dressmaker's on Velvet Street on Tuesday morning, by the front door, in daylight, with a box. In this city, my dear, that is not a gift. That is an announcement."
By the fire, the man in gray had opened his eyes.
He was looking down the long room too. At the silver head by the musicians. And his finger on the side of his tall thin glass had stopped tapping.
And from the doors at the end of the long room, from the hall, a footman in white said something to the Duke, very low, with his eyes on the air above the Duke's head. And the Duke nodded, and turned to Lyra, and said:
"The tenth bell. She's asking for you."
